summary: An excerpt from a novel (Book 1, part 86) mixing two scenes. In the first, a narrator and his colleague Jolu debug code for a program that auto-updates for hundreds of thousands of users, and they decide to keep a new feature secret by limiting invitations to one person each who has been known for at least five years. In the second, the narrator describes the ruins of the Sutro Baths in San Francisco: once the largest indoor bathing house in the world, opened in 1896, burned for insurance in 1966, and now left as a stone labyrinth at Ocean Beach beside dangerous sea caves, with Seal Rock nearby.
one_line: Excerpt from a novel where programmers plan a secret invite rule, followed by a description of the ruined Sutro Baths in San Francisco.
key_facts: The narrator and Jolu debug code together, with Jolu at the keyboard while the narrator watches over his shoulder.
The narrator says the code will be used by hundreds of thousands of people and that users receive updates automatically, usually once a week or so.
The narrator quotes the saying "With enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow."
The narrator proposes that invitees bring a maximum of one person, who must have been known personally for a minimum of five years.
Jolu says the rule "sounds like some awesome 007 stuff."
The narrator recalls their Harajuku Fun Madness days, a game with social challenges involving large groups of people.
The Sutro Baths opened in 1896 and were then the largest indoor bathing house in the world.
The Sutro Baths were a huge Victorian glass solarium with pools, tubs and an early water slide.
The owners torched the Sutro Baths for the insurance in 1966, after the site declined by the fifties.
Today the Sutro Baths remain as a labyrinth of weathered stone set into the cliff-face at Ocean Beach.
Sea caves beside the Sutro ruins let waves rush through and over the ruins in rough tides, and have drowned the occasional tourist.
Ocean Beach lies past Golden Gate Park beside a stark cliff lined with expensive houses.
Seal Rock is a giant white rock off the shore that once hosted sea lions until they were relocated.
